Agent Firewall is a process-level firewall [enforced](https://coder.com/docs/ai-coder/agent-firewall) inside each workspace, restricting whatever AI tool is running there to an explicit allow list of domains and HTTP methods. Every allow or deny decision is logged to the control plane, where it can be exported to a customer's security information and event management (SIEM) system. Both Agent Firewall and AI Gateway [integrate](https://coder.com/solutions/ai-governance) with a customer's identity provider through OpenID Connect (OIDC) and System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM), allowing Coder to tie any given AI action back to a specific authenticated developer.

## Market

### Customer

Coder's target customers are large, security-conscious companies where regulatory requirements prevent source code from leaving the organization's cloud or data center. Coder's self-hosted design [keeps](https://coder.com/solutions/workspaces) source code and data on infrastructure the customer already owns, which lets security teams treat it as an internal deployment rather than a third-party service handling the customer's code. Many of these companies rely on legacy systems that have become expensive or hard to standardize. A virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI), for instance, serves a similar function to Coder’s workspaces by giving each user a configured, centralized desktop operating system. However, a VDI often [assigns](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-desktop/terminology) each developer a dedicated virtual desktop, and those machines typically run [20-24 hours](https://www.island.io/blog/coder-island-vdi-devs) a day, on top of Windows licensing costs.

J.B. Hunt, a freight and logistics company, hosted its remote developers on more than [150](https://coder.com/success-stories/jbhunt) Azure virtual desktop instances before adopting Coder. This approach produced laggy remote sessions, up to two weeks of onboarding time per new hire, and inconsistent setups. After migrating, it cut developer VDI cloud spend by more than [90%](https://coder.com/success-stories/jbhunt), consolidating from over 150 individual VDI environments to a handful running on Kubernetes. Similarly, payabl., a payments company certified to the highest level of the payment card industry's data security standard, cut onboarding time from [one week](https://coder.com/success-stories/payabl) to under one minute and improved resource efficiency by [20%](https://coder.com/success-stories/payabl) by automatically shutting down idle workspaces. Palantir [used](https://coder.com/success-stories/palantir) Coder to reduce environment configuration drift and compile times.

### Market Size

The cloud development environment (CDE) market category is relatively new. In September 2024, CDEs had reached less than [5%](https://coder.com/blog/why-cdes-should-be-on-it-leaders-agendas-insights-from-the-new-gartner-market-gui) of their potential target audience, and [30%](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/coder-launches-cloud-development-environment-140000560.html) of organizations in regulated industries are projected to mandate CDE use for security and compliance by 2028, up from [10%](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/coder-launches-cloud-development-environment-140000560.html) in 2024. In May 2026, a new market guide [defined](https://www.gartner.com/en/documents/7916309) agentic development sandbox platforms as an emerging category.

The budget Coder competes for is moving toward AI coding. Enterprises spent [$4 billion](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/) on AI coding tools in 2025, up from [$550 million](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/) in 2024, and [90%](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-07-01-gartner-identifies-the-top-strategic-trends-in-software-engineering-for-2025-and-beyond) of enterprise software engineers are projected to use AI code assistants by 2028, up from fewer than [14%](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-07-01-gartner-identifies-the-top-strategic-trends-in-software-engineering-for-2025-and-beyond) in early 2024. One estimate put the VDI market, which includes the developer desktops Coder replaces, at [$19.3 billion](https://www.fortunebusinessinsights.com/virtual-desktop-infrastructure-market-107849) in 2025.

The rise in developer headcount drives demand for both AI coding tools and the environments they run in. As of Q3 2025, there were [48.4 million](https://www.slashdata.co/research/developer-population) developers worldwide, with headcount jumping [21%](https://www.slashdata.co/blog/global-developer-population-trends-2025-how-many-developers-are-there) from 2023 to 2024. Each developer running several agents multiplies the environments a platform team has to template and secure.

## Competition

### Competitive Landscape

Coder’s competition can be placed into two categories. The first is the cloud development environment, where it faces browser-based and hosted environments such as [StackBlitz](https://research.contrary.com/company/bolt) and GitHub Codespaces. Most of these run on the vendor's infrastructure, while Coder [runs](https://coder.com/pricing) inside the customer's environment.

The second bucket of Coder’s competitors is a newer layer where AI agents execute code, where venture-backed sandbox providers like Daytona and E2B sell isolated environments for agents through an API, and where model providers have started building or buying the same capability. In 2026, [OpenAI](https://research.contrary.com/company/openai) [acquired](https://ona.com/stories/ona-joins-openai) Ona, formerly Gitpod, and [Anthropic](https://research.contrary.com/company/anthropic) [launched](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-managed-agents-updates) self-hosted sandboxes for its managed agents, with Daytona among the providers.

Coder's differentiation from its competitors is that it governs both humans and agents in one self-hosted system and is not tied to a single model provider. Its workspaces serve human developers as well as agents, and AI Gateway and Agent Firewall [apply](https://coder.com/solutions/ai-governance) the same controls to Claude Code, Codex, or Coder's own agent. Sandbox providers sell execution for agents alone, and model providers' self-hosted options govern only their own agents.

## Business Model

Coder doesn’t provide the compute, storage, and infrastructure that power its customers' workspaces. Customers [provision](https://coder.com/pricing) workspaces on infrastructure they already own, so those costs sit with the customer and Coder's own business is asset-light.

![Coder's pricing page showing three tiers, a free Community plan, a Premium plan billed annually per user that includes AI Governance, and a custom-priced AI Premium plan that removes the cap on active Coder Agents](https://images.prismic.io/contrary-research/CEf3R1sI5gi7JAai_rec-01.png?auto=format%2Ccompress&fit=max&w=3840 "width=2608 | height=1422")

*Source: [Coder](https://coder.com/pricing)*

Coder’s Community plan is [directed](https://coder.com/pricing) toward hobbyists and small teams. It’s free and provides full access to Coder’s open-source core features, including unlimited workspaces, unlimited template creation, access to Coder Agents, and third-party agent compatibility. Premium adds prebuilt workspaces and exclusive access to AI Governance features such as AI Gateway, Agent Firewall, and user auditing, as well as cost control measures like usage quotas.

While Community users can create and store unlimited templates, spinning up a workspace off of a template’s specifications takes time as infrastructure must be provisioned, dependencies installed, and repos cloned. This process can take up to [15 to 20 minutes](https://coder.com/blog/coder-prebuilt-workspaces-beta) in complex cases. Premium, however, enables developers to keep a warm pool of workspaces that start in under [a minute](https://coder.com/blog/coder-prebuilt-workspaces-beta), reducing onboarding time and allowing developers to spawn short-lived workspaces for quick tasks.

![Coder's plan comparison table showing up to five active Coder Agents on Community and Premium and unlimited on AI Premium, with AI Gateway and Agent Firewall available only on the paid tiers](https://images.prismic.io/contrary-research/NAWBJrYE-meOWIpV_rec-02.png?auto=format%2Ccompress&fit=max&w=3840 "width=2156 | height=1128")

*Source: [Coder](https://coder.com/pricing)*

As of October 2026, Coder's pricing page [caps](https://coder.com/pricing) both Community and Premium at five concurrently active Coder Agents across a deployment, while AI Premium removes the cap and adds agents triggered through an API and agent jobs that run in network-isolated workspaces. Five concurrent agents across an entire deployment is a hard ceiling for any team larger than a handful of developers. Coder's licensing documentation [describes](https://coder.com/docs/ai-coder/agents/licensing-usage) one way Premium buyers can exceed it. A Premium license includes a pool of "Agent Time" that lets agents run concurrently until the pool is used up, after which the five-agent cap applies again.

## Key Opportunities

### Sovereign Infrastructure Mandates

Governments and regulators are pushing enterprises to keep software infrastructure under local control. More than [75%](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/10/23/gartner-2026-technology-trends/) of European and Middle Eastern enterprises are projected to move virtual workloads to local options such as sovereign clouds, regional providers, or their own data centers by 2030 to reduce geopolitical risk, up from less than [5%](https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2025/10/23/gartner-2026-technology-trends/) in 2025.

Effective January 2025, the EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act [requires](https://www.eiopa.europa.eu/digital-operational-resilience-act-dora_en) banks, insurers, and other financial entities to [manage](https://www.cssf.lu/en/ict-and-cyber-risk-for-dora-entities/) the risk of their third-party information and communication technology providers. In June 2025, Microsoft [announced](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2025/06/16/announcing-comprehensive-sovereign-solutions-empowering-european-organizations/) a Sovereign Private Cloud designed to run in hybrid or air-gapped environments. As compute moves into these regional and isolated environments, the AI coding agents that run on top of it have to be deployable there too, which a tool offered only as a vendor-hosted service cannot do. Coder already [supports](https://coder.com/docs/install/airgap) air-gapped and offline deployments, and it plans to use part of its [$90 million](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) Series C to expand across Europe, Asia, and North America.

### Governing Agents Beyond Engineering

Identity systems built for human employees and static service accounts are struggling to keep pace with AI agents. A February 2026 industry survey found that more than [16%](https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2026/02/18/token-sprawl-in-the-age-of-ai) of organizations do not track the creation of new AI-related identities and that [24%](https://cloudsecurityalliance.org/blog/2026/02/18/token-sprawl-in-the-age-of-ai) take more than 24 hours to rotate or revoke a credential after potential exposure.

Coder's customers are already extending it past engineering. In April 2026, KKR [said](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) it was extending Coder to analysts, data scientists, and other non-engineering users, and QRT had rolled Coder out to half of its more than [2K employees](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development), a mix of engineers, data scientists, and analysts. As of October 2026, Coder's agents page [frames](https://coder.com/solutions/agents) AI use as already spanning marketing managers, designers, product managers, financial analysts, and HR leaders.

Coder's architecture is suited to this shift because it avoids creating a new credential type to govern. The agent loop [runs](https://coder.com/docs/ai-coder/agents) in the control plane, LLM credentials never enter the workspace, and every agent action is tied to the authenticated user who submitted the prompt. The agent has the same permissions as that user, with no shared bot identity or service account. An analyst's agent has analyst-level access, and an HR manager’s agent has HR-level access. Coder also [integrates](https://coder.com/solutions/ai-governance) with identity providers through OIDC and SCIM and exports audit events to SIEM tools, so it plugs into a customer's existing identity provider.

## Key Risks

### Agent Vendors Running Inside Customer Infrastructure

Coder's main value-add is that it's capable of fully running inside customer infrastructure. In October 2025, GitHub [enabled](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-10-28-copilot-coding-agent-now-supports-self-hosted-runners/) its Copilot coding agent to run on an organization's own self-hosted runners instead of GitHub's cloud sandbox, giving it access to internal resources, such as packages, that are not reachable from the public internet, and in April 2026, GitHub [added](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-04-03-organization-runner-controls-for-copilot-cloud-agent/) organization-level controls to make those runners the default. GitHub does not need to win enterprises away from an existing tool the way Coder does; it only needs to extend governance into a product teams are already using, which erodes the self-hosted argument Coder has used to differentiate from hosted-only competitors like Codespaces.

Model providers are moving the same way. In August 2026, [Anthropic](https://research.contrary.com/company/anthropic) [launched](https://claude.com/blog/run-claude-code-sessions-on-your-own-compute) self-hosted environments for Claude Code in public beta, which run sessions inside the customer's network, and [OpenAI](https://research.contrary.com/company/openai)'s [acquisition](https://ona.com/stories/ona-joins-openai) of Ona brings customer-controlled environments to Codex. Coder's Agent Relay, launched in [September 2026](https://coder.com/blog/introducing-agent-relay-cloud-hosted-agents-self-hosted-execution), runs tool calls from [Cursor](https://research.contrary.com/company/cursor) and Claude Code inside Coder workspaces. If enterprises standardize on one agent vendor and accept that vendor's own self-hosted option, Coder's case narrows to customers that want one control plane across several agents.

### Agent Governance at the Identity Layer

Enterprises may solve agent governance at the identity layer instead of through their development environment provider. In February 2026, Hush Security, a Tel Aviv-based startup, [announced](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/hush-security-launches-the-first-unified-access-management-platform-for-agentic-ai-and-non-human-identities-302695519.html) general availability of its Unified Access Management Platform, which replaces long-lived secrets with scoped, just-in-time credentials tied to verified workload identities. For AI agents, Hush calculates the merged permissions of an agent and the user it acts on behalf of, the same delegated-identity idea Coder uses, applied to downstream resources instead of the workspace.

Larger incumbents have moved to provide similar solutions as well. In August 2026, Okta [announced](https://www.okta.com/newsroom/press-releases/okta-brings-first-class-identity-to-ai-agents-with-agent-sso/) general availability of Agent SSO, which registers AI agents that support its Cross App Access standard as identities in its directory, at no additional cost within core SSO plans used by more than [20K customers](https://www.okta.com/newsroom/press-releases/okta-brings-first-class-identity-to-ai-agents-with-agent-sso/). Okta sells discovery of unregistered agents, named human owners, access certifications, and agent deactivation separately as Okta for AI Agents.

The threat to Coder is about budget ownership. Identity teams already control the budget and vendor relationships that agent governance would draw from, and Coder's own product [integrates](https://coder.com/solutions/ai-governance) with identity providers through OIDC and SCIM, so those vendors sit upstream of it. If enterprises decide that discovery, ownership, and access policy for agents belong in the identity layer, Coder's remaining role narrows to runtime containment.

### Supply Chain Exposure Through Coder's Registry

In [August 2026](https://coder.com/blog/coder-registry-security-incident-what-happened-and-what-to-do), an attacker used a compromised Cloudflare API key to redirect part of the traffic to Coder's module registry for 14 hours, serving tampered modules designed to steal cloud credentials. Coder [said](https://coder.com/blog/coder-registry-security-incident-what-happened-and-what-to-do) its codebase and Google Cloud infrastructure were not compromised. Self-hosted deployments that pulled modules from that registry were still exposed to a server Coder, not the customer, controlled. Coder's pitch to security-conscious buyers rests on keeping code and credentials inside the customer's perimeter, so a repeat incident in its own supply chain would undercut the case that sets it apart from hosted alternatives.

## Summary

AI coding agents are moving into enterprise development quickly, with a KKR managing director stating in April 2026 that more than [80%](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) of enterprise developers were using or planning to use them. It raised a [$90 million](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) Series C led by KKR in April 2026 and reported that bookings grew [300%](https://coder.com/blog/90m-series-c-led-by-kkr-to-advance-secure-enterprise-ai-development) in the year before the round. As GitHub, [Anthropic](https://research.contrary.com/company/anthropic), and [OpenAI](https://research.contrary.com/company/openai) add self-hosted execution and governance to their own agents, the open question is whether enterprises keep paying for an agent-agnostic control plane once each agent vendor offers its own.

## Portainer - About the company

Portainer is a series A company based in Auckland (New Zealand), founded in 2017 by Neil Cresswell and Anthony Lapenna. It operates as a Developer of container management software for orchestrating modern infrastructure deployments. Portainer has raised $7.2M in funding from investors like Bessemer Venture Partners, Movac and AmpliPHI Ventures. The company has 188 active competitors, including 36 funded and 11 that have exited. Its top competitors include companies like Red Hat, Spectro Cloud and Komodor. 

### Company Details

Developer of container management software for orchestrating modern infrastructure deployments. This platform provides centralized control for Docker, Kubernetes, and edge computing environments. It facilitates governance, role-based access control, and automated configuration for distributed software fleets. The technology supports offline-first operations for industrial settings and integrates with Git workflows for standardized deployment processes. Operational teams utilize these tools to visualize clusters, monitor container status, and implement security policies across multiple nodes. By abstracting the complexity of underlying orchestrators, the software enables consistent management of containerized applications in cloud, on-premises, and remote industrial locations.

Tiger Data, formerly Timescale, develops PostgreSQL-based database technology, including TimescaleDB for time-series data and the Tiger Cloud managed service. Its tools support workloads such as telemetry, real-time analytics, and AI applications, with capabilities for time-series processing and vector search. The company also provides infrastructure and developer tools for running and managing database-backed applications.

* Metadata

    + May 7, 2025
    + in [News](https://textual.textualize.io/blog/category/news/)
    + 2 min read

# The future of Textualize

Textual has come a *long* way since I figured why not build an application framework on top of [Rich](https://github.com/Textualize/rich).

Both were initially hobby projects. I mean look how much fun I was having back then:

> Making good progress with Textual CSS.   
>   
> Here's a "basic" app. The [\#Python](https://twitter.com/hashtag/Python?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) \+ CSS in the screenshots generates the layout in the terminal here.  
>   
> Separating the layout and design from the runtime logic will make it easy to create gorgeous TUI apps. 🤩 [pic.twitter.com/Rxnwzs4pXd](https://t.co/Rxnwzs4pXd)
> 
> — Will McGugan (@willmcgugan) [November 25, 2021](https://twitter.com/willmcgugan/status/1463977921891217411?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Working on Textual has been a constant source of delight; figuring out how to make a terminal do things that it shouldn't really be able to do, and to a lesser extent a source of frustration when working around the baffling edge cases in emulators and the terminal protocol.

But work around it we did, and now Textual is an awesome piece of software that has spawned a community of developers building TUIs for [all kinds of things](https://github.com/textualize/transcendent-textual) (not to mention, [web apps](https://github.com/Textualize/textual-serve))!

Additionally, Textual has some of the [best docs](https://textual.textualize.io/guide/screens/) for any Open Source project. Shout out to [@squidfunk](https://x.com/squidfunk) and [@pawamoy](https://x.com/pawamoy) for the tech that makes these beautiful docs possible.

Ultimately though a business needs a product. Textual has always been a solution in search of a problem. And while there are plenty of problems to which Textual is a fantastic solution, we weren't able to find a shared problem or pain-point to build a viable business around. Which is why Textualize, the company, will be wrapping up in the next few weeks.

Textual will live on as an Open Source project. In the near term, nothing much will change. I will be maintaining Textual and Rich as I have always done. Software is never finished, but Textual is mature and battle-tested. I'm confident transitioning from a full-time funded project to a community project won't have a negative impact.

## Thanks![¶](https://textual.textualize.io/blog/2025/05/07/the-future-of-textualize/#thanks "Permanent link")

I'd like to thank the awesome devs I worked with at Textualize, and the many developers that followed along, contributing and building apps. Wether you were an early adopter or you just discovered Textual, you made Textual what it is today.

## Get in touch[¶](https://textual.textualize.io/blog/2025/05/07/the-future-of-textualize/#get-in-touch "Permanent link")

If you would like to talk Textual, feel free to find me on our [Discord server](https://github.com/textualize/textual/) or the socials.

I've also started a [blog](https://willmcgugan.github.io/) where I will write a little more on this from a more personal perspective.

May 14, 2025

Today we're announcing [NanoCo (creators of NanoClaw)](https://www.linkedin.com/company/nanocoai?trk=public_post-text), our enterprise offering from the team behind NanoClaw, and a $12M seed round led by [Valley Capital Partners](https://www.linkedin.com/company/valley-capital-partners?trk=public_post-text), with participation from [Docker, Inc](https://www.linkedin.com/company/docker?trk=public_post-text), [Vercel](https://www.linkedin.com/company/vercel?trk=public_post-text), [monday.com](https://il.linkedin.com/company/mondaydotcom?trk=public_post-text), [Hugging Face](https://www.linkedin.com/company/huggingface?trk=public_post-text)'s Clem Delangue, and many more incredible investors from across the industry.

NanoClaw brought sandboxed agents, human-in-the-loop approvals, and vault-backed security to hundreds of thousands of developers. 

NanoCo brings that same foundation to the enterprise, giving every employee their own professional assistant that plugs straight into their tools, learns how they work, and gets the job done with them. 

Over time, agents evolve, adapt to your style, and become the kind of assistant, as Singapore's Foreign Minister put it, you wouldn't dare switch off.

Huge thanks to our community and investors for helping us get to where we are today. NanoClaw will remain free, stable, and open source. NanoCo is just an additional chapter in our story — an assistant for every employee, built on what got us here in the first place. 

We can't wait to show you what we've got 💪

## post by dae 1 day ago

[![](https://sea2.discourse-cdn.com/flex002/user_avatar/forums.ankiweb.net/dae/48/65_2.png "width=48 | height=48")](https://forums.ankiweb.net/u/dae)

[dae](https://forums.ankiweb.net/u/dae)

[1d](https://forums.ankiweb.net/t/regarding-recent-events/74723 "Post date")

Full disclosure up front: the deal I made with AnkiHub requires them to pay me over time. They’ll only be able to do that if Anki remains profitable. That makes me hesitate to post this, because it’s in my best interests that Anki do well.

A couple of weeks ago, AnkiHub released an AnkiMobile update that accidentally broke things for a significant number of users, and they are now rushing to address the issues that have been reported.

The affected users are frustrated, and rightly so - this was a fumble that should not have happened, and it’s caused a loss of trust. AnkiHub have acknowledged that they dropped the ball, but I share in the blame here: I still work with them behind the scenes, and had more of my attention been on AnkiMobile’s release, perhaps some of this frustration could have been avoided.

When I reflect on the way the management transition was handled on my end, I’m ashamed that I did not handle it better. Ideally it would have been done over a longer time frame, giving the community time to get to know the AnkiHub team, and for things to transition over smoothly. Sadly, that’s not how it worked out - I rushed the transition through because I was really struggling to hold on any longer.

My sudden public absence and that lack of a smooth transition has not made things easy for AnkiHub. They have had to hit the ground running without a starting base of goodwill, and some of the community have been quick to assume every misstep is malice or gross incompetence.

One area where I think people are particularly off-base is the implication that AnkiHub are profiteering off open-source contributions or out to make a quick buck. The reality is quite different: the founders have not paid themselves a cent from AnkiMobile’s proceeds. They have built up a bigger team than I ever managed to, and between their greater expenses and instalments to me, they are unlikely to see any profit from Anki until at least 2030.

I have worked quite closely with Andrew, Nick and members of their team since the transition happened, and I still genuinely believe their hearts are in the right place. I have been saddened by the way some members of the community always assume their intentions are bad, and I worry about the negative effect the infighting will have if it continues.

Ultimately though, a lot of that fear/mistrust has come about because of my rushed exit. I’m really sorry that I didn’t handle it better at the time, and for the effect it has had on the community.

Current feedback in many instances explained by people projecting the frustration accumulated elsewhere and assuming a trend from insufficient data, but this kind of reaction should naturally subside *as long as* further updates indeed take the course of taking feedback into account and correcting things.

[![](https://sea2.discourse-cdn.com/flex002/user_avatar/forums.ankiweb.net/dae/96/65_2.png "width=48 | height=48")](https://forums.ankiweb.net/u/dae)

[dae](https://forums.ankiweb.net/u/dae)

[Feb 2](https://forums.ankiweb.net/t/ankis-growing-up/68610 "Post date")

Hi all,

Anki’s 19th birthday was about 4 months ago. It would have been a good time to pause and reflect on what Anki has become, and how it will grow in the future. But I ended up letting the moment come and go, as I didn’t feel like I had the free time. It’s a feeling that’s been regrettably common of late, and I’ve come to realise that something has to change.

For a number of years, I’ve reached out to some of the most prolific contributors and offered them payment in exchange for them contributing more code or support to Anki. That has been a big help, and I’m very grateful for their contributions. But there is a lot that I haven’t been able to delegate. With no previous management experience, I was a bit daunted by the thought of seeking out and managing employees. And with so much to get on with, it always got put in the “maybe later” basket.

As Anki slowly grew in popularity, so did its demands on my time. I was of course delighted to see it reaching more people, and to have played a part in its success. But I also felt a big sense of responsibility, and did not want to let people down. That led to unsustainably long hours and constant stress, which took a toll on my relationships and well-being.

The parts of the job that drew me to start working on Anki (the ‘deep work’, solving interesting technical problems without constant distractions) have mostly fallen by the wayside. I find myself reactively responding to the latest problem or post instead of proactively moving things forward, which is neither as enjoyable as it once was, nor the best thing for the project.

There have been many offers to invest in or buy Anki over the years, but I’ve always shut them down quickly, as I had no confidence that these investment-focused people would be good stewards, and not proceed down the typical path of enshittification that is unfortunately so common in VC and PE-backed ventures.

Some months ago, the AnkiHub folks reached out to me, wanting to discuss working more closely together in the future. Like others in the community, they were keen to see Anki’s development pace improve. We’ve had a symbiotic relationship for years, with their content creation and collaboration platform driving more users to Anki. They’ve managed to scale up much faster than I did, and have built out an [impressive team](https://www.ankihub.net/about-us).

During the course of those talks, I came to the realisation that AnkiHub is better positioned to take Anki to the next level than I am. I ended up suggesting to them that we look into gradually transitioning business operations and open source stewardship over, with provisions in place to ensure that Anki remains open source and true to the principles I’ve run it by all these years.

This is a step back for me rather than a goodbye - I will still be involved with the project, albeit at a more sustainable level. I’ve spent 19 years looking after my “baby”, and I want to see it do well as it grows up.

I’m confident this change will be a net positive for both users and developers. Removing me as a bottleneck will allow things to move faster, encourage a more collaborative approach, and free up time for improvements that have been hard to prioritise, like UI polish. It also means the ecosystem will no longer be in jeopardy if I’m one day hit by a bus.

It’s natural to feel apprehensive about change, but as the benefits become clearer over the coming months, I suspect many of you will come to wish this change had happened sooner.

Thank you to everyone who has contributed to making Anki better up until now. I’m excited for Anki’s future, and can’t wait to see what we can build together in this next stage.

# Vectify AI Raises £1.1M to Automate Document and Financial Data Analysis

£1.1M

Vectify AI has raised £1.1 million to develop its AI software for document and financial data analysis, enabling businesses and financial professionals to extract structured insights from large volumes of unstructured documents and financial data without manual processing.

Vectify AI, a UK artificial intelligence company, has raised £1.1 million to develop its AI-powered platform for document and financial data analysis. The company is building software that enables businesses and financial professionals to automatically extract, structure, and analyse information from large volumes of unstructured documents and financial datasets — transforming raw document inputs into the structured, queryable data that supports informed decision-making without requiring manual data entry or processing.

Document-heavy workflows are one of the most persistent sources of operational inefficiency in financial services, legal, compliance, and corporate functions. Contracts, financial statements, regulatory filings, due diligence materials, correspondence, and transaction records contain enormous volumes of relevant information — but in a form that is designed for human reading rather than for machine processing. Extracting specific data points from these documents — covenant terms from a loan agreement, financial metrics from an income statement, key dates from a contract — requires either manual review that is slow and expensive, or the kind of sophisticated natural language processing and document understanding that has only recently become accessible through large language models.

Vectify AI's platform applies large language models and document understanding AI to these workflows, enabling users to define the data they want to extract from a class of documents and have the platform apply that extraction consistently across large document volumes. For financial analysis, the platform can process sets of financial statements, extract key metrics, and produce structured datasets that can be directly fed into financial models or analytical tools without manual data entry. For contract review and due diligence, it can identify and flag specific clause types, extract key terms, and produce summary outputs that reduce the time legal and commercial teams spend on routine document review.

The funding will be used to develop the platform's document understanding and data extraction capabilities, build integrations with document management and financial analysis tools, and grow the commercial pipeline.

# 

# A Year Ago, We Raised $3M

Hi, I'm Anoop.

About a year ago, Bruno raised $3M, and we didn't announce it at the time.

That wasn't an accident. Actions speak louder than words, and it’s much harder to build trust through actions. So instead of making a big announcement when the funding closed, we decided to keep building.

Over the last year, we've continued to grow rapidly. We've expanded the team, invested heavily in the product, and seen adoption continue to grow across startups and large enterprises alike.

More importantly, we've stayed focused on the principles that got us here in the first place.

## What Hasn't Changed

Developers choose Bruno because it was different.

**Local-first** versus cloud-first.

**Git-native** versus proprietary collaboration/versioning.

**Open formats** versus lock-in.

**Simple** versus bloated.

Those ideas resonated with developers because they're not features. They're beliefs about how developer tools should work.

The funding hasn't changed those beliefs. If anything, it's allowed us to invest more aggressively in them.

## Building for the Long Term

From the beginning, our goal has been to build a sustainable project that can serve developers for decades.

For us, that's thinking beyond short-term growth:

* **Building products that developers genuinely enjoy using.**
* **Creating more value over time, then expanding access to it.**
* **Growing by expanding the pie, not by creating more restrictions.**
* **Making decisions that strengthen trust over time.**

Over the last year, after raising funding, we didn’t move more features behind a paywall.

Instead, we made several previously paid features free for everyone, including gRPC support, WebSocket support, response visualization, terminal mode, and file mode.

That matters because trust is built through choices, not statements. We believe sustainable businesses are built by creating more value, not by creating more restrictions. As Bruno grows, we want all developers to benefit from the work we do, not just the ones that pay us.

That philosophy continues to guide us today.

## What We're Investing In

Our goal isn't to build a giant platform or recreate the complexity that many developers came to Bruno to escape.

Today, developers use Bruno through:

* Bruno Desktop
* Bruno CLI
* VS Code integration
* Self-hosted API documentation
* GitHub integrations
* OpenCollection

[OpenCollection](https://www.opencollection.com/) is a big part of where we're investing.

Our goal is simple: create an open, developer-friendly format for API workflows that works naturally with Git and the rest of the software development lifecycle.

Not another proprietary standard or another cloud dependency. Just a simple, portable way to define and share API workflows. The same philosophy that shaped Bruno continues to shape OpenCollection.

Open, transparent, and developer-first.

## Why Silverton

We spoke with a number of investors before making a decision.

[Silverton Partners](https://www.silvertonpartners.com/) stood out because they shared our long-term perspective, have a track record of being founder-first, and are a local resource for our co-founder Ryan Reynolds in Austin, Texas.

We weren't looking for a partner that would push us toward short-term growth at all costs. We wanted people who understood our commitment to building durable products, supporting developers, and thinking in decades rather than quarters.

That alignment mattered more than the capital itself.

## Looking Ahead

The last few years have exceeded anything we imagined when we started Bruno. We've built an incredible team and a product developers genuinely love.

And we've built a business that gives us the opportunity to think long term.

This investment helps us accelerate what we're already doing: improving the core product, investing in OpenCollection, expanding our tooling, and continuing to build software that fits naturally into developer workflows.

To everyone who has used Bruno, contributed to the project, shared feedback, reported bugs, written documentation, or trusted us with your workflows: thank you.

We're excited for what comes next.

**Anoop, Ryan, and Team Bruno**
